questions.question: What is the most useful beginner mental model for an MLflow experiment?
options: It is a deployed prediction endpoint.
It is a logical container that groups comparable runs for one ML task.
It is the object store that holds model weights.
It is a replacement for a training framework.
questions.explanation: An experiment organizes runs. Each run records one execution's parameters, metrics, tags, inputs, and artifacts; deployment is a separate responsibility.

questions.question: A run logs accuracy and hyperparameters but no dataset reference or code version. What production question remains unanswered?
options: Whether the run has a numeric metric
Which data and code produced the model artifact
Whether MLflow can display the experiment name
Whether the model has a registry version number
questions.explanation: Metrics describe an outcome, not its provenance. Dataset identity and immutable code identity are required to reconstruct the evidence chain.

questions.question: Why log a model signature and input example with an MLflow Model?
options: They replace model evaluation.
They define and demonstrate the inference contract that loading or serving can validate.
They grant users permission to the artifact store.
They make every dependency deterministic.
questions.explanation: A signature describes expected inputs, outputs, and parameters, while an input example makes the contract concrete and supports serving-payload checks.

questions.question: Why should evaluation and promotion be separate pipeline steps?
options: Evaluation computes evidence; promotion applies policy and changes a registry reference only after all gates pass.
MLflow cannot store evaluation metrics.
Promotion must happen before a model is packaged.
Evaluation is useful only after 100 percent rollout.
questions.explanation: Separating measurement from the state-changing decision makes thresholds, approvals, and failures reviewable and prevents a successful evaluation call from implying production readiness.

questions.question: Which registry URI follows the current alias-based workflow?
options: models:/renewal/Production
runs:/renewal@champion
models:/renewal@champion
experiments:/renewal/champion
questions.explanation: Model stages are deprecated. A registered model alias is addressed as models:/<model-name>@<alias>, such as models:/renewal@champion.

questions.question: What is the safest deployment handoff for a mutable champion alias?
options: Every serving request resolves the alias again.
The deployment controller resolves the alias once, records the immutable version, and rolls out that version.
Every worker chooses any recent model version.
The training notebook directly edits production routing.
questions.explanation: Resolving once creates a stable deployment unit and prevents workers from silently diverging when an alias moves during a rollout.

questions.question: Why can proxying artifact access through the tracking server simplify security?
options: Clients no longer need direct object-store credentials, so artifact access can be centralized.
It removes the need for TLS and authentication.
It makes all artifacts public by default.
It guarantees the serving endpoint is healthy.
questions.explanation: With proxied artifacts, the server owns storage credentials and clients use the tracking endpoint. Teams still need authentication, authorization, TLS, network controls, and audit logs.

questions.question: What should a self-hosted team do before running an MLflow database schema upgrade?
options: Delete old runs so the migration is faster.
Move champion to the newest candidate automatically.
Back up the backend, test the migration and client matrix, and prepare rollback or restore procedures.
Run different schema versions on the same database concurrently without testing.
questions.explanation: Official guidance notes that schema migrations can be slow and are not guaranteed to be transactional. Backup, rehearsal, compatibility tests, and restoration planning contain the risk.
